planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in autumn for natural cold-moist stratification and spring emergence, or plant divisions into dry-mesic, humus-rich woodland soil beneath deciduous canopy.

directions: Buckley's goldenrod is a Piedmont and lower-mountain woodland species found in dry-mesic oak-hickory forests from Virginia and North Carolina south into Georgia and Alabama, where it grows in the dappled light of upland slopes rather than open fields. It is one of the latest-blooming goldenrods, often flowering well into October and November with small, sparse-rayed yellow heads carried on slender stems above rough, narrow leaves. Its tolerance of dry shade and leaf litter makes it a good choice for naturalizing under established hardwoods where other sun-loving goldenrods fail, and the very late bloom extends nectar availability for bees and flies into the first frosts.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for cold stratification, or set divisions in spring into moist, rich soil along a partly shaded woodland edge or floodplain thicket.

directions: Ontario aster is a wide-ranging Midwestern and Great Lakes native found along river floodplains, moist thickets, and the shaded edges of bottomland woods, often growing where spring flooding keeps the soil consistently damp. It produces lanky, slightly hairy stems topped with abundant small, pale lavender-blue flowers from September into October, providing late nectar in semi-shaded transitional habitats where few other asters persist. Because it tolerates periodic wet feet and partial canopy, it suits rain gardens, streambank plantings, and the moist fringe between lawn shade and open sun. Give it room to spread, as it forms loose colonies via rhizomes and self-seeding over time.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall to allow natural cold-moist stratification, or plant divisions in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in a mesic cove-forest setting.

directions: Thinleaf aster grows in rich, mesic cove and slope forests of the Appalachian Mountains from Pennsylvania south to Georgia and Alabama, favoring the broken light found under a hardwood canopy with good humus content. It carries pale lavender to nearly white ray flowers on slender, often zigzagging stems above thin, lightly toothed leaves in late summer and fall. It is well suited to shaded native plant gardens and woodland borders where it can mingle with ferns and spring ephemerals that have finished their display by the time it flowers. Established plants spread modestly by short rhizomes and tolerate the leaf-litter buildup typical of forest floors.
sources: Weakley's Flora of the Southeastern United States

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold-moist stratification, or plant divisions in spring into consistently moist soil along a partly shaded streambank or floodplain border.

directions: Tradescant's aster is a northeastern native found along riverbanks, floodplain thickets, and moist low woods from New Brunswick and Quebec south to Pennsylvania, where it roots in alluvial soil that stays damp for much of the growing season. It is among the latest-blooming asters, often flowering into late October with airy, branching sprays of small white flowers on wiry stems. Its tolerance for streamside shade and periodic inundation makes it a useful choice for naturalized rain gardens and wooded stream buffers, where its fine texture and late nectar supply complement coarser-leaved companions like joe-pye weed and woodland sunflower.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for cold stratification, or plant divisions into lean, well-drained soil under an open conifer canopy; established plants tolerate dry shade once rooted.

directions: Western showy aster inhabits dry, open ponderosa pine and Douglas-fir forests of the inland Pacific Northwest, from British Columbia south through Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and western Montana, growing in the partial shade of scattered conifers. It bears unusually large, showy violet-blue ray flowers for the genus atop rough, hairy stems and broad basal leaves, blooming in mid to late summer. Its drought tolerance once established and preference for lean, rocky duff make it well suited to dry woodland gardens and naturalized plantings under mature pines where moisture-hungry perennials struggle. It spreads slowly from a woody rootstock rather than aggressively colonizing.
sources: Burke Herbarium Image Collection (University of Washington)
